text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning
HELSINGIN SANOMAT

- Defence Minister Anneli Taina said Finland may need to reassess its stance on membership of NATO before the next general elections in 1999. At present, Finland is not seeking to join the western alliance.
- Skanska bought building rights to Helsinki property from Tradeka-yhtyma and plans to build 700 flats in a project worth about half a billion markka. @
- Finance ministry's Kari Nars says the ministry has capability to buy currency needed to service Finland's debt directly from the market.
- Finland's wolf population numbers 140 -- too small -- expert group says.
- Gale-force winds kept Silja Line's Silja Festival from entering the port of Tallinn on Tuesday.
- AIDS support centre says condoms should be free of value-added tax.
- Upturn in building activity is finally starting to show in Finnish metal industry demand. @
KAUPPALEHTI
- Banks say they never promised trade union members free bankcard services. Unions say banks are raising service charges against an earlier agreement.
- Payment of wages in euro will probably begin during the 1999-2002 transition period on the basis of company-specific agreements, says finance ministry's Rauno Niinimaki.
- European Commission to review UPM-Kymmene's acquisition of the Finnpap marketing association for compliance with competition rules. @
- Japanese-owned sawmill Misawa Homes of Finland plans to raise capacity from 30,000 to 75,000 cubic metres in three years.
DEMARI
- Finland is EU's model pupil -- the only member to comply with all social directives of the Union.
AAMULEHTI

- Further cuts in social security could lead to unrest and create a need for tens of thousands of armed guards to keep people safe, says Esa Swanljung, head of the Confederation of salaried employees STTK.
- Police want powers to impersonate drug purchasers. @
TURUN SANOMAT
- Police commissioner Jaakko Sonck has suggested drug tests for all asylum seekers following recent arrest of drug dealers at a refugee centre.
--John Acher, Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 235
